column4: The section says the source word غاشية names the Hour as a cover that comes over creation; Yusuf's warning asks whether people feel safe from غاشية من عذاب الله, making the same arriving cover an explicit punishment.
The section's Ghashiya root becomes bodily visible when fire covers the faces of people whose clothing is tar; it shows how an outer covering can overwhelm the face.

The source section names Ghashiya as an encompassing cover; here dark pieces of night cover wrongdoers' faces (أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ), turning night-cover into punishment opposite the garden's shelter.
The same covering verb named in the section describes punishment closing over people from above and beneath their feet; it completes the all-around movement of the Ghashiya image.
The section's covering root is used of the smoke that covers people (يَغْشَى النَّاسَ); smoke becomes another enveloping form of punishment.
The section's Ghashiya covering has a matching form in the coverings over Hell's people (غَوَاشٍ مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ), with bedding below and covers above turning enclosure into torment.
Fire canopies stand above and below Hell's people; this gives the section's crushing cover a two-sided counterpart to the garden's protective growth.
The verse says waves cover people like canopies (غَشِيَهُم مَوْجٌ كَالظُّلَلِ); the cover is lethal danger, and so sharpens the section's distinction between an oppressive and a protecting cover.
The same cover word named for Ghashiya appears as a veil over disbelievers' sight (غِشَاوَةٌ) alongside great punishment; it connects covering the truth with covered perception.
The garden people say God protected them from the scorching torment (وَوَقَانَا عَذَابَ السَّمُومِ); this is the section's clearest example of the garden's covering as a shield against heat.

The section's dictionary describes Paradise as a reward hidden from people today; this verse says no soul knows what has been hidden for them as delight (أُخْفِيَ لَهُم), making that concealment part of the promised garden's appeal.
After saying the person was heedless, God removes his covering (غِطَاءَكَ) and his sight becomes sharp; this reverses the section's cover that reaches inward to understanding.
The section's dictionary gives fainting as an inward effect of being covered; here the trumpet makes those in the heavens and earth fall stunned, then they rise at the next blast.
The section's covering root is used when drowsiness comes over a group (يَغْشَى طَائِفَةً مِّنكُمْ نُعَاسًا); it gives the inward, consciousness-covering side of the image in a scene of fear.
Sleep comes over the believers as security (النُّعَاسَ أَمَنَةً) before rain strengthens them; it shows a covering of consciousness that protects, unlike the overpowering cover of punishment.
The angels ask God to protect believers from Hell and admit them to gardens; this joins the section's two covers in one passage, protection from torment and entry into the garden.
The people of Shu'ayb receive the punishment of the Day of the Shade (عَذَابُ يَوْمِ الظُّلَّةِ); a shade becomes an enveloping punishment rather than the garden's refuge.
The condemned are given garments of fire (ثِيَابٌ مِّن نَّارٍ); the image reverses an ordinary covering that conceals or protects into one that torments.
God gives garments that protect people from heat and from violence (سَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ الْحَرَّ); this names the protective work that the section's garden-cover performs, against its searing fire.
The people of the left are in scorching wind and boiling water; this establishes the heat against which the section's protected garden offers shelter.
Their shade is black smoke (ظِلٍّ مِّن يَحْمُومٍ), an enclosing shade that carries torment rather than protection.
The verse says that this shade is neither cool nor generous (لَا بَارِدٍ وَلَا كَرِيمٍ); it explicitly denies the sheltering benefit the section hears in the garden's cover.
The condemned are sent toward a shade with three branches (ظِلٍّ ذِي ثَلَاثِ شُعَبٍ); the following verse denies that it shades or protects, reversing the section's garden-cover.
This verse says that shade does not protect from the flame (لَا ظَلِيلٍ وَلَا يُغْنِي مِنَ اللَّهَبِ); it directly contrasts the source section's shield-like garden.
The promised garden's food and shade endure (أُكُلُهَا دَائِمٌ وَظِلُّهَا); this gives the section's sheltering garden a lasting quality against transient coverings.
The garden's people rest in shade without seeing sun or bitter cold; its protection from exposure makes concrete the section's garden as a covering refuge.
The Quran names the garden at the Lote Tree as the Garden of Refuge (جَنَّةُ الْمَأْوَىٰ); this brings out the sheltering sense of the section's garden and shield dictionary branches.

The section's dictionary labels the farmer as a coverer of seed; this verse uses الكُفَّار for cultivators whose rain-grown plant first delights, then dries and crumbles, making the seed-covering branch and its transience visible.

The verse compares the believers to a crop that sends out shoots and thickens, delighting its sowers; it shows the growth possible beneath a covering soil, which the section contrasts with covering truth so nothing grows.
A single grain produces seven ears and multiplies its yield; read beside the section's farmer-covering-seed branch, it gives a concrete image of what hidden growth under soil can become.

A garden owner says he does not think his orchard will ever perish; beside the section's hidden, lasting Garden, his visible garden exposes the false security of treating an earthly cover as permanent.
The owner's fruit is encompassed by ruin (أُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِ); the failed orchard contrasts with the section's garden as a protecting and hidden reward.
Noah's son expects a mountain to shield him from the flood, but the wave comes between them; this reverses the section's assurance that God protects the garden people from overwhelming punishment.
A cloud approaches and is mistaken for rain, but proves to be a wind carrying painful punishment; the apparent covering from the sky becomes a threat rather than provision.
The fire's enclosure surrounds those who do wrong (سُرَادِقُهَا); it supplies another explicit image of punishment hemming people in, like the section's covering calamity.

After their nakedness appears, Adam and his spouse fasten leaves of the Garden over themselves (مِن وَرَقِ الْجَنَّةِ); here garden growth literally conceals exposed bodies, a distinct counterpart to trees covering the ground.
The verse says clothing is given to cover people's nakedness (لِبَاسًا يُوَارِي سَوْآتِكُمْ); it extends the section's ordinary covering image from a saddle cloth to bodily concealment.
The oath by night uses the section's covering verb (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا); it is a direct occurrence of the night-cover image that the section traces across roots.
The oath names night when it covers (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ), the same night-cover image the section hears in Ghashiya and in its other root branches.
God covers the day with night (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ); this makes the section's night-as-cover image cosmic and recurrent.
The same covering verb describes night covering day (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), repeating the section's physical image in a passage about God's signs.
The verse pictures God wrapping night over day and day over night (يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ); it makes the section's covering motion a recurring cosmic turning.
God darkens the night and brings out the morning light; this gives the covered night a visible boundary, when the light that it hid returns.
Night is made a garment (اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا), a direct clothing image for the cover the section traces through night and Ghashiya.
Night is made a garment and sleep a rest (اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا وَالنَّوْمَ سُبَاتًا), joining the section's covering night to the inward quiet of sleep before the day resumes.

When night covers Abraham (جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ), the section's named garden root appears in another branch with the same concealing image; the star's setting then makes the cover part of Abraham's rejection of transient objects.
God strips the day from the night (نَسْلَخُ مِنْهُ النَّهَارَ), leaving people in darkness; this gives the night-cover image its opposite motion, light removed rather than night laid over it.

Moses falls stunned when the mountain crumbles at the manifestation of his Lord; this is a concrete instance of the inward collapse that the section's fainting dictionary branch places beside an outer cover.
On the Day, faces are humbled before the Living and Sustaining One (وَعَنَتِ الْوُجُوهُ); it closely parallels the section's low, subdued faces.
Their eyes are humbled and humiliation overwhelms them (تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ); this joins the lowered face to an affliction that covers, as in the section's judgment scene.
Hearts tremble on that Day; this supplies the inward fear behind the humbled eyes in the next verse and the section's externally visible submission.
Eyes are humbled (أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ), paralleling the section's humbled faces; the preceding verse 79:8 contributes the fear within that becomes visible in the eyes.
The disbelievers emerge from graves with humbled eyes (خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ); it gives another judgment-day counterpart to the section's humbled faces.
On the Day some faces turn white and others black (تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ); the split face-scene contrasts with the two kinds of faces in the section.
The white-faced people are in God's mercy and remain there; this gives the section's pleasant garden-side faces a specific judgment-day counterpart to the darkened faces of the previous verse.
Some faces on that Day are bright (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُّسْفِرَةٌ); this begins a face-by-face contrast that clarifies the section's divided outcomes.
Those bright faces are laughing and rejoicing; their visible ease contrasts with the humbled faces in the section.
Other faces have dust upon them (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ); the material covering makes the section's face-cover image concrete.
Darkness overwhelms those faces (تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌ); this completes the covered, degraded face opposite the bright face in 80:38.
Some faces on that Day are radiant (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ); they parallel the section's pleasant faces against the humbled ones.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord (إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ); their orientation adds a distinct posture to the bright side of the section's face-scene.
Other faces are gloomy (وَوُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَاسِرَةٌ), the opposite bodily state to the section's pleasant faces.
Those gloomy faces expect a calamity to break them; this names the inward dread behind the lowered and burdened faces of the section.
Fire sears their faces (تَلْفَحُ وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ), a direct bodily counterpart to faces covered by fire in the section, with the verse adding their grimace.
Wrongdoers are brought near the Fire, humiliated and watching furtively; this extends the section's humbled face into an exposed, fearful posture before punishment.
On the Day the faces of those who lied about God are blackened; this ties a disbelieving stance to the darkened face that contrasts with the section's garden faces.

The verse says coverings lie over disbelievers' hearts so they cannot understand (أَكِنَّةً أَن يَفْقَهُوهُ); it gives a cognitive counterpart to the section's dictionary image of an event covering understanding.
Coverings over hearts prevent understanding and heaviness affects the ears; this closely matches the section's movement from an outer cover to perception and thought.
The speakers say their hearts are in coverings from the message (قُلُوبُنَا فِي أَكِنَّةٍ); this makes cognitive concealment an expressed response to truth.

A hidden barrier is placed between the Prophet and those who do not believe in the Hereafter when the Quran is recited; it is another specific veil on reception, distinct from the heart-cover in the section.
God places a covering over the sight of one who follows desire as a god, alongside a seal on hearing and heart; this joins outer sight and inward judgment as the section's cover image does.
The speakers describe their own hearts as wrapped (قُلُوبُنَا غُلْفٌ); their claimed closedness gives another form of the section's inner-cover image around refusal.

Their hearts are in a covering of heedlessness about the revelation (فِي غَمْرَةٍ مِّنْ هَٰذَا); this is a distinct word for a mind submerged from what it should perceive, like the section's fainting branch.
What they earned has rusted over their hearts (رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِم); this gives a concrete image of wrongdoing accumulating as an inner veil.
The verse asks why people clothe truth in falsehood and conceal it while knowing (تَلْبِسُونَ الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ); it spells out the section's dictionary claim that kufr covers truth.
Those who hide clear proofs and guidance after its disclosure enact the section's dictionary branch of disbelief as covering what is true.
On that Day nothing about the people is hidden (لَا تَخْفَىٰ مِنكُمْ خَافِيَةٌ); it marks the boundary where every worldly concealment is removed.
When all come forth, nothing about them is hidden from God; this gives the exposed opposite of the section's enveloping and concealing covers.
The Day secrets are tested and brought out (تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ); it shows inward concealment opening, a boundary to the section's cover over understanding.
